bib.title: GAP: Graph-Based Agent Planning with Parallel Tool Use and Reinforcement Learning

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "GAP: Graph-based Agent Planning with Parallel Tool Use and Reinforcement Learning", Jiaqi Wu, Qinlao Zhao, Zefeng Chen, Kai Qin, Yifei Zhao, Xueqian Wang, Yuhang Yao (Tsinghua, HUST, NUS, CMU). Preprint, arXiv 2510.25320v1, 29 Oct 2025 (marked "Preprint", no venue).

COVERAGE: 39,885 of 39,885 chars read (12 pages, including references, related work, and the prompt template and case study in Appendix B). Nothing skipped. Extraction is clean except figure internals and the table layout, which are noted under PROBLEMS.

FIT WARNING: Moderate. The topic fits: plan a dependency DAG, run independent tools in parallel, and compare against sequential ReAct-style tool use on turns, time, and accuracy. But the evidence is thin and narrow:
- It covers one 3B model and one tool (Wikipedia search).
- The comparison is against trained Search-R1-style sequential models, not prompted ReAct.
- Accuracy gains are small and there are no seeds or variance.
- The abstract says "dramatic improvements in tool invocation efficiency", but the paper reports turns, time, and length, and never counts tool calls.
Use it as one illustrative training result, not as general evidence that parallel planning beats ReAct.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. GAP cuts LLM interaction turns versus Search-R1, the sequential baseline.
 number: HotpotQA 1.78 vs 2.27 turns (21.6% reduction). 2Wiki 2.03 vs 3.05 (33.4%). Table 2 gives Search-R1 as 2.69 and 3.05 turns on these two sets.
 setup: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, SFT then RL, 2018 Wikipedia with E5 retrieval. The sample size for Table 2 is not stated.
 quote: "On HotpotQA, GAP requires only 1.78 turns compared to Search-R1's 2.27 turns (21.6% reduction), while on 2Wiki, the reduction is even more pronounced (2.03 vs. 3.05 turns, 33.4% reduction)."
 where: p7, Section 5.2.
 Caveat: the 2.27 in the text is the turn count that Table 2 lists for AFM-RL-3B, not Search-R1. Against Search-R1's 2.69 in the table, the reduction is about 34%. The paper's 21.6% figure is really GAP vs AFM-RL (1.78 vs 2.27). This is an internal inconsistency.

2. GAP cuts wall-clock time.
 number: HotpotQA 168 s vs 248 s (32.3%). 2Wiki 206 s vs 262 s (21.4%).
 setup: same as above. "Time cost" is the time to infer a batch of data, and the batch size is not given.
 quote: "GAP achieving 32.3% and 21.4% time cost reductions on HotpotQA (168 vs. 248s) and 2Wiki (206s vs. 262s), respectively."
 where: p7.
 Caveat: 248 s and 262 s are the AFM-RL-3B figures in Table 2, so the comparison is against AFM-RL, not Search-R1. Search-R1 is 221 s and 254 s. Against Search-R1 the savings are about 24% and 19%.

3. Response length is shorter.
 number: 24.9% on HotpotQA (416 vs 554 tokens). 20.3% on 2Wiki (452 vs 567).
 quote: "reduce response length by 24.9% on HotpotQA (416 vs. 554 tokens) and 20.3% on 2Wiki (452 vs. 567 tokens)"
 where: p8.
 Caveat: 554 and 567 are again the AFM-RL-3B numbers. Search-R1 is 584 and 651.

4. Accuracy gain is small.
 number: GAP-3B averages +0.9% over the best baseline across the four multi-hop sets. +3.95% over Search-R1.
 setup: Table 1, Exact Match, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct.
 quote: "outperforming the best baseline by 0.9% on average across four multi-hop datasets (HotpotQA, 2Wiki, Musique, Bamboogle)."
 where: p7.
 Table 1 (GAP-3B vs AFM-RL-3B vs Search-R1):
 - HotpotQA 42.5 / 41.1 / 37.6
 - 2Wiki 41.7 / 39.8 / 31.7
 - Musique 18.7 / 19.0 / 15.1 (AFM-RL is higher)
 - Bamboogle 43.8 / 43.2 / 37.1
 - NQ 39.6 / 39.3 / 38.3
 - TriviaQA 59.1 / 58.2 / 59.3 (Search-R1 is higher)
 - PopQA 40.1 / 42.4 / 43.5 (GAP is lower than both)
 The wins over AFM-RL are 0.6 to 1.9 points, with no variance reported.

5. Table 2 accuracy differs from Table 1.
 number: Table 2 HotpotQA Acc is 36.7 (GAP), 35.7 (AFM-RL), 25.3 (Search-R1). Table 1 gives 42.5, 41.1, 37.6. 2Wiki matches across tables (41.7, 39.8, 31.7).
 quote: "GAP-3B (Ours) 36.7 416 168 1.78"
 where: p8, Table 2.
 Not explained by the paper. Treat HotpotQA accuracy with caution.

6. Cost-of-pass (Figure 2) shows GAP-3B as best on accuracy and cost on HotpotQA.
 number: none in the text. The values are only in the plot.
 quote: "GAP-3B achieves the best balance with highest accuracy at lowest cost."
 where: p7.

7. Training data and method.
 number: about 7,000 trajectories. Synthesised with GPT-4o from NQ and HotpotQA. Kept only if the task needs at least 3 searches. Parallel to sequential mix of 6:4. Length of about 2,000 tokens or less.
 quote: "approximately 7,000 high-quality training trajectories were generated through trajectory synthesis and quality filtering."
 where: p5, Section 4.1.
 Training is SFT cold start (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, observation-masked loss) followed by DAPO RL via VeRL. The reward is binary exact-match correctness only: "scoreanswer ∈ {0,1}". There is no efficiency reward. The latency gains come from the model learning to batch, not from being rewarded for it. The abstract mentions RL on "strategically sampled queries", but the body does not describe the sampling.

BASELINES (matched?): Partly.
- Compared: Search-R1, ZeroSearch, StepSearch (taken from other papers, so Table 1 cells may come from different setups; StepSearch has gaps), AFM-RL-3B (Chain-of-Agents), and the untrained Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct.
- Plain ReAct is not run. The paper says "traditional ReAct baselines", but the sequential baselines are RL-trained TIR models, not prompted ReAct.
- No ablation of graph vs flat parallel search. There is no "parallel | search without a plan" arm, and no SFT-only vs SFT+RL comparison.
- The paper says four model configurations, but only 3B is shown.
- The efficiency tables (Table 2) cover only HotpotQA and 2Wiki.
- The GAP SFT data is distilled from GPT-4o using a multi-agent system, and the baselines may not have equal data.

LIMITS
- The authors concede little beyond future work on multi-objective rewards.
- Only one model size (3B) and only retrieval-QA. Other tools named in the formalisation (calculator, python) are not tested.
- The dependency graph is generated by the model and is not checked for correctness. No analysis of wrong graphs.
- No tool-call counts, no parallel-width stats, and no cost-of-pass numbers in the text.
- No variance, seeds, or sample counts.
- The "up to 33.4%" turn claim relies on the mismatched baseline figure (see claim 1).
- The abstract says "significantly outperforms", yet the average gain is +0.9.
- Parallel-vs-sequential trade-off against the context window is mentioned but not measured.
- The text says it "determines parallelizability autonomously", but there is no test on queries that are purely sequential, aside from the 40% sequential share in the training data.

BUILDS ON: ReAct (Yao et al. 2023). Search-R1 (Jin et al. 2025). Chain-of-Agents / AFM (Li et al. 2025). DAPO (Yu et al. 2025). VeRL/HybridFlow (Sheng et al. 2025). Cost-of-pass (Erol et al. 2025). ToRL, SimpleTIR, ARPO, WebThinker, ZeroSearch, StepSearch. Datasets: NQ, HotpotQA, TriviaQA, PopQA, 2Wiki, Musique, Bamboogle, set up following Search-R1.

CODE (verbatim)
- Graph output format (p4, Section 3.2):
<graph>
<node id="s1">search("capital of France")</node>
<node id="s3" depends="s1">search("population of {s1}")</node>
</graph>
- Parallel search syntax (Table 3 prompt, p12): "Execute independent tasks in parallel by using | separator in <search>."
- Algorithm 1 (p5): Phase 1 generates the plan and parses the graph, then calls TopologicalSort(G) to get levels. Phase 2 executes level by level, running {o_j = T(q_j)} in parallel and appending <observation>. Phase 3 generates the answer.
- Tags: think, plan, search, observation, reflection, answer. Full prompt template in Table 3 (p12). A worked case, Frankenheimer and DeBartolo, in Table 4 (p12).

FIGURES
- Figure 1 (p3): "Illustration of Graph-based Agent Planning paradigm..." It shows the query turning into subtasks with "Depend On" fields, then parallel searches, then aggregation. This is the best candidate for the chapter, because it shows the DAG plan and parallel batch faster than prose.
- Figure 3 (p8): turns CDF and response length. GAP mostly finishes within 2 turns; Search-R1 typically takes 3-6.
- Figure 2 (p7): accuracy vs cost-of-pass, HotpotQA.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found in the PDF.
- Figure internals, such as the plot values, are not extractable, and the Table 1 bolding is lost in the text.
- Section 3.3 formulas and equation numbering are broken in places (the reward is "(10)", cost-of-pass shows "Cm(p)Rm(p)" where a ratio is intended).
- Numbers are mismatched between prose and Table 2 (see claims 1 to 3).
- The text says "four model configurations", but only the 3B model appears.
- The training description mentions "child threads", which does not match the rest of the paper (likely text reused from another paper).
- The abstract claims about tool-call efficiency are not backed by tool-call counts.
